1830.name: Solid, liquid, gas states and changes of state
1830.description: This unit covers the properties of solids, liquids, and gases using the particle model, including gas pressure. It explains changes of state in terms of the particle model while developing skills in using appropriate techniques, apparatus, and materials in lab work.
1830.why: This unit builds on pupils’ prior learning from Introduction to states of matter and changing states, where they explored how solids, liquids, and gases change when heated or cooled. It develops their understanding of the particle model, focusing on how particles behave and interact during changes of state, including gas pressure and motion. This positions pupils to deepen their knowledge in the next unit, Solutions, where they will apply these concepts to understand the behaviour of mixtures and how they can be separated, further reinforcing the thread of substance interactions.

1930.name: Solutions

This prepares pupils for the next unit, Separation techniques, where they will apply their understanding of mixtures and solutions to learn how substances can be separated, deepening their grasp of the interactions and properties of materials.

1932.name: Separation techniques
1932.description: This unit covers techniques for separating mixtures, including filtration, evaporation, distillation, and chromatography, as well as identifying pure substances. Conduct experiments safely, record observations, evaluate methods, and suggest improvements.
1932.why: This unit builds on pupils’ prior learning from Properties, changes and separating materials, where they explored material properties and methods of separation. It focuses on techniques like filtration, evaporation, and distillation to separate mixtures based on their properties. 1931.name: Atoms, elements and compounds
1931.description: This unit explores the basic atomic model, the differences between atoms, elements, and compounds, and the varying physical and chemical properties of elements. It covers chemical symbols, formulae, SI units, and IUPAC nomenclature, emphasising their use in describing elements and compounds.

This prepares pupils for the next unit, Understanding chemical reactions, where they will apply this knowledge to explore how atoms rearrange during chemical reactions, reinforcing the principles of matter and its transformations.

1933.name: Understanding chemical reactions
1933.description: This unit covers the conservation of mass in changes of state and chemical reactions, including atom rearrangement. 1934.name: Earth's resources
1934.description: This unit explores Earth's composition, structure, and rock cycle, including the formation of igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks. It also examines Earth as a source of limited resources and the importance of recycling, alongside skills in making and evaluating observations and measurements.
1934.why: This unit builds on pupils’ prior learning from Rocks and soils, where they explored the formation and classification of rocks and the composition of soils. It deepens their understanding by examining Earth's resources, including how these materials are used and the importance of sustainable management. This prepares pupils for the next unit, Carbon cycle and climate change, where they will apply their knowledge to understand the role of Earth's resources in global cycles and the impact of human activity on climate, reinforcing the need for responsible resource use.

1935.name: Fuels and energetics

12348.outcome: I can investigate the change in pH on adding base to a fixed volume of acid.

12356.name: Bonding to carbon atoms

12381.name: Discovery and uses of carbon nanostructures
12381.outcome: I can describe the scientific discovery process and relate the uses of nanostructures to their properties, structure and bonding.
points: Scientists discovered and isolated fullerenes accidentally, which led to exciting new possibilities in chemistry.
Research into the allotropes of carbon is an important part of chemistry's history, earning multiple Nobel Prizes.
Graphene is so thin that it's nearly transparent, allowing most light to pass through.

12361.name: Hydrocarbons
12361.outcome: I can describe alkanes and represent the first four by name, molecular formulae and displayed formulae.

12362.outcome: I can compare the sizes of microscopic and submicroscopic ‘particles’ using scientific notation, as well as discuss a variety of applications using nanoparticle technology.

A chemical reaction between an acid and base to produce a neutral solution of a metal salt and water.
When a substance dissolves in a liquid, it is described as soluble in that liquid.

12303.name: Atomic structure (electron mass of 0.0005)
12303.outcome: I can describe the physical characteristics of atoms, protons, neutrons and electrons.
points: Electrons have a relative charge of -1 and roughly a relative mass of 0.0005.
Protons are found in the atomic nucleus, have a relative electric charge of +1, and a relative mass of 1.
Neutrons are found in the atomic nucleus, have no electric charge, and a relative mass of 1.
An atom has no electric charge and contains equal numbers of protons and electrons to balance the charge.
The atom has a nucleus surrounded by electrons, with the nuclear radius much smaller than that of the atom.
keywords: An electron is a subatomic particle with a negative charge and a very small relative mass of 1/1835 (negligible).
A neutron is a subatomic particle with no charge and a relative atomic mass of 1.
A nucleus is found in the centre of an atom. It consists of protons and neutrons. It is significantly smaller in size than the atom.
A proton is a subatomic particle with a positive charge and a relative atomic mass of 1.
Anything that is smaller than an atom. There are three subatomic particles called electrons, protons and neutrons.

1129.name: Developing a model for atoms (Geiger and Marsden)
1129.outcome: I can describe the structure of atoms, the sub-atomic particles they contain, and developments leading to this model.
points: The atomic model has changed over time.
Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford (Geiger and Marsden), Bohr and Chadwick have all suggested atomic models.
The plum pudding model of the atom & the nuclear model are two important models in the history of the atom's discovery.
New evidence from the scattering experiment led to a change in the atomic model.
keywords: Model of the atom with a small positive charge in the centre surrounded by a cloud of orbiting electrons. The atom is mostly empty space.
Model of the atom showing that negative electrons are embedded in a ball of positive charge.
A stream of positive alpha particles fired through a thin piece of gold foil. This lead to an update of the atomic model, from the plum pudding model to nuclear model.

1133.name: Atoms, elements and compounds (mass number to 1 d.p.)
1133.outcome: I can describe elements as being made up of only one type of atom, and that elements can combine chemically to form compounds.
points: Atoms of every element consist of the same three subatomic particles.
All elements consist of their own atoms, with a unique number of protons defining the element.
Everything around us is made of different combinations of atoms, either on their own, or in compound form.
We use element symbols in formulae as a common language to share chemical compositions.
keywords: An atom is the building block of all matter.
The chemical composition tells you the different types of atoms in a chemical.
The chemical formula of a molecule is a shorthand way of listing the type and number of atoms in a compound.
A compound is made of two or more different elements chemically bonded together.
Each element is made up of only one type of atom.

1131.name: Modern periodic table with electron configuration
1131.outcome: I can describe the way the modern periodic table is organised and draw the electronic configuration of the first twenty elements.
points: The periodic table is ordered by increasing atomic number (proton number).
The periodic table is split into periods and groups.
The position of an element in the periodic table is linked to its atomic number and the arrangement of its electrons.
Elements can be classed as metals or non-metals according to their position on the periodic table.
A useful model for atoms arranges electrons in shells around the nucleus.

of an atom of an element describes how the electrons are arranged in shells.
To group things is to put similar things together.
A period is a row on the periodic table that corresponds to the number of electron shells in an atom.

1126.name: Atomic number and mass number (RAM 1 d.p.)
1126.outcome: I can relate the atomic number and mass number to the structure of atoms of each element.
points: The atomic number of an element states the number of protons in the nucleus of every atom of that element.
The number of electrons in an atom is equal to the number of protons in the nucleus of the atom.
The mass number of an element is about equal to the number of protons and neutrons in atoms of that element.
keywords: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, which determines the element's identity.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
RAM is the mean mass of an atom relative to 1/12th the mass of an atom of carbon–12.

1127.name: Isotopes and nuclear notation
1127.outcome: I can write and use the standard nuclear notation for different elements and their isotopes.
points: Atoms of many elements vary in the exact number of neutrons in their nucleus, and each version is called an isotope.
Existence of isotopes results in relative atomic masses of some elements not being whole numbers.
Standard nuclear notation shows the chemical symbol, the mass number and the atomic number of the isotope.
keywords: An atom of an element with the same number of protons, but different mass numbers due to different numbers of neutrons.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
A neutron is a subatomic particle with no charge and a relative atomic mass of 1.
A proton is a subatomic particle with a positive charge and a relative atomic mass of 1.

1130.name: Relative formula mass (mass number to 1 d.p.)
1130.outcome: I can calculate the relative formula mass of substances using data taken from a periodic table.
points: The relative atomic mass is the mean mass of an atom compared to 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
The relative formula mass (RFM or Mr) is the sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in a chemical formula.
%mass of an element in a compound = (relative mass of element in compound ÷ RFM of compound) × 100
keywords: RAM is the mean mass of an atom relative to 1/12th the mass of an atom of carbon–12.
(RFM or Mr) is the sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in a chemical formula.

1218.name: History of the periodic table
1218.outcome: I can describe the development of the periodic table and explain its current form.
points: Dalton (1803) arranged known elements in order of atomic weights.
Newlands (1865) noticed that every eighth element, in order of atomic mass, repeated similar properties.
Mendeleev swapped the order of atomic weights in order to fit elements better into groups of similar properties.
Mendeleev’s periodic table had gaps and he predicted missing elements that were later found.
Mendeleev was not aware of isotopes, so was unable to explain why the ordering by atomic weight was not always correct.
keywords: A scientist who devised the periodic table of elements.
The historical name for atomic mass, i.e. the ratio of the mass of an atom compared to a standard.
An atom of an element with the same number of protons, but different mass numbers due to different numbers of neutrons.
RAM is the mean mass of an atom relative to 1/12th the mass of an atom of carbon–12.

1497.name: Why chemical reactions occur
1497.outcome: I can explain chemical bonding in terms of the transfer or sharing of electrons.
points: There are five different types of substance: monatomic, simple covalent (molecules), giant covalent, ionic and metallic.
The outer shell in most atoms can hold 8 electrons but, in hydrogen and helium, it can only hold 2 electrons.
Most atoms increase their stability by forming bonds with other atoms so that they have a full outer shell of electrons.
Some atoms will share electrons with other atoms to increase their stability.
Some atoms will lose or gain electrons to increase stability forming cations or anions, respectfully.
keywords: Made up of two or more atoms chemically bonded together. These are usually non-metal atoms.
When an atom has a full outer shell of electrons, it has a noble gas electron configuration.
The outer shell is the highest energy level in an atom and is usually the furthest from the nucleus.

1496.name: Forming ions for ionic bonding (RAM 1 d.p.)
1496.outcome: I can use electron configuration diagrams (and notation) to explain how positive and negative ions are formed for ionic bonding.
points: Atoms are more stable when they have a full outer shell.
Metal atoms become more stable when they lose the electron(s) in their outer shell, and become positive ions (cations).
Non–metal atoms become more stable when they gain electrons to fill their outer shell and become negative ions (anions).
Ions form through the loss or gain of electrons.
Standard ion notation uses superscript charge values where the charge follows the number (e.g. 2+, not +2).
keywords: Used to show how chemical bonds are formed between atoms – the electrons from one atom are shown as dots and the electrons from the other atom are shown as crosses.
An ion is an atom or group of atoms with a positive or negative charge due to the loss or gain of electrons.

12323.name: Comparing types of chromatography: including gas chromatography
12323.outcome: I can identify features of different types of chromatography and describe how the techniques are used to separate and identify components of a mixture.
points: Paper, thin layer (TLC), and gas chromatography (GC) can all distinguish between pure and impure substances.
Chromatographic processes use a mobile and stationary phase. TLC and GC both use silica/alumina as a stationary phase.
Thin layer chromatography (TLC) uses locating agents to develop chromatograms and aid analysis of them.
Chromatograms from gas chromatography (GC) also provide details about the amount of each component in a sample.
Retention factors (Rf) and retention times both provide quantitative information about a sample's components.
keywords: A chromatogram is the resultant pattern on the stationary phase after chromatography has been carried out.
A type of chromatography that uses an inert substance packed into a coiled tube as the stationary phase and an unreactive/inert gas as the mobile phase.
The movement of a solvent and any dissolved components of a sample along the stationary phase in chromatography.
A surface along which the solvent (and any dissolved components) travels. It does not move during chromatography.
A type of chromatography that uses a thin layer of an inert substance spread over an unreactive flat surface as the stationary phase and a liquid state substance for the mobile phase.

1228.name: Mass in a chemical reaction (RAM 1 d.p.)
1228.outcome: I can use conservation of mass and relative formula masses to predict the mass of unknown products or reactants.
points: In a chemical reaction, the atoms in reactants are rearranged and are the same atoms that are in the products.
The mass of products in a chemical reaction is equal to the mass of the reactants.
The sum of the RFM of the reactants equals the sum of the RFM of the products, taking account of balancing coefficients.
keywords: A constant numerical multiplier of the variables in a term.
A reaction using a symbol equation with coefficients to ensure there are equal numbers of atoms of each element on both sides of the equation.
Conservation of mass means that the combined mass of the starting reactants equals the combined mass of the products formed.
(RFM or Mr) is the sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in a chemical formula.

12333.name: Predicting states of matter and limitations of the particle model
12333.outcome: I can use the particle model to predict the state of matter of a substance at different temperatures and discuss the limitations of this model for explaining how particles behave.
points: There are changes in arrangement, movement and energy of particles during state changes.
There are two types of change; physical and chemical, and the physical state of a substance can be predicted.
The attraction between particles has a role in determining the amount of energy needed for state changes.
The particle model has limitations, for example by showing particles as same sized, inelastic spheres.
The model does not show the attraction between the particles which affects the amount of energy needed to change state.
keywords: Occurs when a reaction takes place and atoms or ions in the reactants are rearranged to make new products/substances.
A point at which we cannot use the model to help us explain a scientific phenomena.
the idea that all objects are made of tiny particles that are in constant motion
A change in which no new substances are formed, such as a change in state, e.g. melting.

(RFM or Mr) is the sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in a chemical formula.

points: One type of fuel cell contains hydrogen that reacts with oxygen from the air to produce a voltage.
Hydrogen used in fuel cells can be extracted from fossil fuels or produced by electrolysis powered by the National Grid.
Other fuel cells exist, but have other products than just water.
There are many strengths and weaknesses of fuel cells, and these should be compared against other energy sources.
keywords: a high voltage transmission system for getting electricity to where it is needed
natural substances that were formed over millions of years ago from the buried remains of ancient organisms. They include coal, oil and gas
a device that produces a voltage when supplied with a fuel and oxygen

12389.name: Transition metals
12389.outcome: I can describe the physical and chemical properties and some uses of transition metals, and compare them to Group 1 metals.
points: Transition metals are generally stronger, harder, more dense and have higher melting points than Group 1 metals.
Transition metals react slowly with water or don’t react with it at all.
Transition metals are often catalysts that speed up chemical reactions.
Transition metals can form ions with different charges and their compounds often exhibit vibrant colours.
keywords: a chemical that speeds up the rate of a reaction without itself being used up.
The mass per cubic metre (m³) or cubic centimetre (cm³) of a material.
An ion is an atom or group of atoms with a positive or negative charge due to the loss or gain of electrons.
refers to a metal element placed in the block between Groups 2 and 3 in the periodic table.

11632.name: Corrosion and its prevention
11632.outcome: I can describe corrosion in detail, including chemical equations, and describe what actions can be taken to prevent corrosion.
points: Corrosion is a general process of degradation of metals through various causes.
Rusting is a specific type of corrosion, affecting iron in the presence of air and moisture.
A metal oxide layer can protect the underlying metal if the oxide forms a physical barrier.
Some coatings are reactive and contain a more reactive metal to provide sacrificial protection, e.g. zinc to galvanise.
Electroplating can be used to improve the appearance and/or the resistance to corrosion of metal objects.
keywords: when a metal reduces in size due to a chemical reaction
a process that uses electricity to deposit a thin layer of metal onto the surface of another conductive object
refers to the corrosion of iron or steel, in the presence of water and oxygen
Using a more reactive metal to corrode preferentially, to protect another metal from corrosion.
The process by which a thin, discoloured layer forms on the surface of a metal due to reactions with the environment, e.g. oxidation.

12391.name: Introduction to reversible chemical reactions
12391.outcome: I can describe reversible chemical reactions, represent them using chemical equations, and give examples.
points: Different types of arrows (→, ⇌) are used in chemical equations to indicate the nature of the reaction.
Reversible reactions are symbolised using the double-headed arrow (⇌) in chemical equations.
In a reversible reaction, both the forward and reverse reactions can occur under the right conditions.
hydrated copper sulfate (blue) ⇌ anhydrous copper sulfate (white) + water
ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride
keywords: A salt that does not contain any water molecules in the crystal structure, e.g. anhydrous copper(II) sulfate (CuSO₄).
Used to show that a chemical reaction is reversible.
A salt that contains water molecules within its crystal structure, shown by a dot in its formula, e.g. hydrated copper(II) sulfate (CuSO₄·5H₂O).
A chemical reaction where the reactants form products that, in turn, react together to reform the reactants.
Used to show the direction of an (irreversible) chemical reaction, showing that reactants form products.

12390.name: Chemical equilibrium
12390.outcome: I can explain the concept of chemical equilibrium and the characteristics of a system in which equilibrium is established.
points: At equilibrium, both reactants and products are formed at the same rate.
Amounts of reactants and products remain constant at equilibrium.
Equilibrium can only occur in a closed system.
keywords: is one in which matter cannot enter or leave the observed environment, allowing only energy transfer between the system and its surrounding environment.
occurs in a closed system when the forward and backward reactions of a reversible chemical reaction occur at the same rate; and the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
is the speed with which a chemical reaction takes place, measured by the amount of a reactant used or amount of product formed in a given time.

12393.name: Industrial equilibria: Haber Process
12393.outcome: I can describe the Haber Process for the production of ammonia, explain the significance of equilibrium in this industrial process, and describe the conditions used.
points: In a reversible reaction the desired product needs to be continuously removed from the reaction.
Natural gas is a feedstock for industrial production of ammonia.
Hydrogen, one of the raw materials in ammonia production, is produced from natural gas and steam.
In industry, the Haber process is typically performed at 150-300 atmospheres, 400-450°C, with an iron catalyst.
Ammonia production is energy-intensive and releases large amounts of carbon dioxide, contributing to global emissions.
keywords: an industrial method for producing ammonia.
Raw materials used in chemical processes to produce other substances.
A mixture of gases which are rich in hydrocarbons, consisting largely of methane.
a natural material in its original state

11638.name: Percentage yield and atom economy
11638.outcome: I can perform calculations related to various aspects of industrial processes, and explain decision-making about the chosen reaction pathways in those processes.
points: In an ideal chemical reaction, all atoms in the reactants would end up in useful products, with no waste.
The theoretical yield of a chemical reaction can be calculated from the reaction equation alone.
The percentage yield shows how actual yield compares with theoretical yield.
Atom economy is a measure of the efficiency with which a reaction uses its reactants.
Many factors will be considered when choosing a reaction pathway.
keywords: is the actual amount of product obtained from a chemical reaction
is the percentage, by relative mass, of reactants that are converted into useful products
is the actual yield (mass of product obtained) divided by the theoretical yield (maximum mass of product possible), as a percentage
is the maximum calculated mass of product expected to form from a given mass of reactants

11637.name: Equilibrium: balance between rate, safety, environment and economics
11637.outcome: I can describe how various factors influence the reaction conditions for industrial equilibria, and understand the trade-offs between production rate, equilibrium position, safety, and cost.
points: Industrial equilibria involve a trade-off between production rate and equilibrium position.

Low temperatures slow reactions but can favour desired product in exothermic reactions.

a manufacturing method where a product is constantly produced

An ionic compound, usually formed by neutralisation of an acid by a base.

11633.outcome: I can compare the properties of glass, clay ceramics, polymers, composites, and metals; and explain how the properties of materials are related to their uses.

numerical information that can be measured or counted

12369.outcome: I can write half-equations and balanced ionic equations.
points: Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons.
Half equations can be written to show which species are oxidised and which are reduced.
Ionic equations can be written for displacement reactions.
keywords: A half equation is a chemical equation used to show the electrons lost in oxidation or the electrons gained in reduction.
A type of reaction in which oxygen bonds to elements of the reactants.
A redox reaction is a reaction where both reduction and oxidation occur.
when an artist takes away a material rather than builds up layers of materials

1802.name: Alternative methods of extracting metals: phytomining and bioleaching
1802.outcome: I can describe how metals are extracted by phytomining and bioleaching and compare different methods of metal extraction.
points: In phytomining, metal is extracted from a crop of plants that absorb metal ions through their roots.
In bioleaching, metal is extracted from bacteria that extract metal from an ore.
Electrolysis is a process used to separate metals from their compounds.
There are advantages and disadvantages associated with each method of extracting metals.
keywords: Bioleaching is a method of extracting metals by growing bacteria on low-grade ores to produce a leachate.
displacement at a point of a wave is the distance that the wave medium is from its rest position.
a process that uses electricity to break down a compound
An ore is a rock that contains metals or metal compounds. A low-grade ore contains a lower percentage of metal or metal compound than a high-grade ore.
Phytomining is a method of extracting metals by growing plants in soil containing low-grade ore.

12378.name: Ionic equations: reactions of Group 1 and Group 7
12378.outcome: I can write balanced ionic equations and half equations for the reactions of Group 1 and 7 elements.
points: Reduction is the gain of electrons, and oxidation is the loss of electrons.
Displacement reactions are often examples of redox reactions.
Half equations show which elements are oxidised, and which are reduced.
keywords: A half equation is a chemical equation used to show the electrons lost in oxidation or the electrons gained in reduction.
a balanced equation showing all the ions involved in a reaction
A type of reaction in which oxygen bonds to elements of the reactants.
A redox reaction is one in which a substance is oxidised and another is reduced.
when an artist takes away a material rather than builds up layers of materials

12415.name: Half equations: electrolysis
12415.outcome: I can write half–equations and balanced ionic equations.
points: A half–equation describes what happens to one reactant in a reaction, such as the process at an individual electrode.
Half–equations show balanced charges as well as balanced atoms.
A balanced ionic equation shows all reacting ions involved in a reaction.
Ions not involved in a reaction do not appear in a balanced ionic equation.
keywords: a chemical equation used to show the electrons lost in oxidation or the electrons gained in reduction
a balanced equation showing all the ions involved in a reaction
A type of reaction in which oxygen bonds to elements of the reactants.
when an artist takes away a material rather than builds up layers of materials
the ions not involved in a chemical reaction

6099.name: Corrosion and its prevention: including half equations
6099.outcome: I can describe corrosion in detail, including chemical equations, and describe what actions can be taken to prevent corrosion.
points: Corrosion is a general process of degradation of metals through various causes.
Rusting is a specific type of corrosion, affecting iron in the presence of air and moisture.
A metal oxide layer can protect the underlying metal if the oxide forms a physical barrier.
Some coatings are reactive and contain a more reactive metal to provide sacrificial protection, e.g. zinc to galvanise.
Electroplating can be used to improve the appearance and/or the resistance to corrosion of metal objects.
keywords: when a metal reduces in size due to a chemical reaction
a process that uses electricity to deposit a thin layer of metal onto the surface of another conductive object
refers to the corrosion of iron or steel, in the presence of water and oxygen
Using a more reactive metal to corrode preferentially, to protect another metal from corrosion.
The process by which a thin, discoloured layer forms on the surface of a metal due to reactions with the environment, e.g. oxidation.

11630.name: Factors affecting equilibrium
11630.outcome: I can explain how changes in pressure, temperature and concentration, as well as addition of catalysts, affect the equilibrium position of a reversible reaction.
points: Catalysts, pressure, temperature & concentration of solutions can affect equilibrium position of a reversible reaction.
If the conditions of a reversible reaction are changed, the equilibrium will move to counteract that change.
A catalyst increases the rate at which equilibrium is achieved.
Increasing temperature increases the rate of both reactions; equilibrium shifts in favour of the endothermic reaction.
Increasing the concentration or pressure of a substance increases the rate of reaction; equilibrium shifts in response.
keywords: states that if a dynamic equilibrium is disturbed by changing the conditions, the equilibrium position ‘shifts’ to counteract the change.
occurs in a closed system when the forward and backward reactions of a reversible chemical reaction occur at the same rate; and the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
refers to the relative concentrations of reactants and products in a reversible reaction at equilibrium.
is the speed with which a chemical reaction takes place, measured by the amount of a reactant used or amount of product formed in a given time.

11644.name: Condensation polymerisation
11644.outcome: I can explain the basic principles of condensation polymerisation.
points: Condensation polymerisation requires monomers with two functional groups.
Condensation polymers can be made of two different monomers.
A polyester is formed by reaction of a monomer with two carboxylic acid groups with a monomer with two alcohol groups.
In condensation polymerisation as well as the polymer a small molecule is formed, usually water.
Amino acids contain two functional groups and can form polypeptides and proteins.
keywords: Addition polymerisation is a type of polymerisation where monomers join together to form only one product; a polymer.
Condensation polymerisation is a type of polymerisation where monomers join together to form a polymer and a small molecule such as water.
Polyamides are condensation polymers formed from monomers containing carboxylic acid and amine groups. They contain amide bonds.
Polyesters are condensation polymers formed from monomers containing carboxylic acid and alcohol groups. They contain ester bonds.
Polypeptides are condensation polymers formed from amino acids. They contain peptide bonds.

11619.name: Alternative methods of extracting metals: phytoextraction and bioleaching
11619.outcome: I can describe how metals are extracted by phytoextraction and bioleaching and compare different methods of metal extraction.
points: In phytoextraction, metal is extracted from a crop of plants that absorb metal ions through their roots.
In bioleaching, metal is extracted from bacteria that extract metal from an ore.
Electrolysis is a process used to separate metals from their compounds.
There are advantages and disadvantages associated with each method of extracting metals.
keywords: Bioleaching is a method of extracting metals by growing bacteria on low-grade ores to produce a leachate.
displacement at a point of a wave is the distance that the wave medium is from its rest position.
a process that uses electricity to break down a compound
An ore is a rock that contains metals or metal compounds. A low-grade ore contains a lower percentage of metal or metal compound than a high-grade ore.
Phytoextraction is a method of extracting metals by growing plants in soil containing low-grade ore.

2159.name: Industrial equilibria: Contact Process
2159.outcome: I can describe the Contact Process for the production of sulfuric acid, explain the importance of each step, and describe the conditions used.
points: The Contact Process involves the production of sulfur trioxide (SO₃) from sulfur dioxide (SO₂) using a catalyst.
The process has three main stages: burning sulfur to produce SO₂, converting SO₂ to SO₃, then converting SO₃ to H₂SO₄.
The conversion of SO₂ to SO₃ is a reversible reaction performed at 1-2 atmospheres and 450°C, using a V₂O₅ catalyst.
Sulfuric acid production is energy-intensive and releases large amounts of CO₂, contributing to global emissions.
Sulfuric acid is vital for various industries, such as: fertilisers, chemical manufacturing, and petroleum refining.
keywords: an industrial method for producing sulfuric acid.
a substance that causes damage by chemical action, often resulting in severe injury or destruction
When a substance transfers energy out to the surroundings by heating, e.g. condensing and freezing.
Raw materials used in chemical processes to produce other substances.
a natural material in its original state

6100.name: Percentage yield and atom economy (RAM 1 d.p.)
6100.outcome: I can perform calculations related to various aspects of industrial processes, and explain decision-making about the chosen reaction pathways in those processes.
points: In an ideal chemical reaction, all atoms in the reactants would end up in useful products, with no waste.
The theoretical yield of a chemical reaction can be calculated from the reaction equation alone.
The percentage yield shows how actual yield compares with theoretical yield.
Atom economy is a measure of the efficiency with which a reaction uses its reactants.
Many factors will be considered when choosing a reaction pathway.
keywords: is the actual amount of product obtained from a chemical reaction
is the percentage, by relative mass, of reactants that are converted into useful products
is the actual yield (mass of product obtained) divided by the theoretical yield (maximum mass of product possible), as a percentage
is the maximum calculated mass of product expected to form from a given mass of reactants
is a chemical product that is desired or valuable

9912.belief: The particles are embedded in the substance.
9912.statement: Students think that the particles are embedded in the substance
9912.correction: Ensure that students are reminded that all matter is made of small particles and nothing is between the particles.

5331.belief: Particle spacing can be overemphasised at the expense of particle movement.
5331.statement: Particle spacing can be overemphasised at the expense of particle movement.
5331.correction: Ensure pupils understand that although particles can move over each other, the forces of attraction mean that the particles are touching.

779.belief: All the Bunsen is hot, flames are the same temperature.
779.statement: All the Bunsen is hot, flames are the same temperature.
779.correction: Ask pupils to explain why they are able to turn the collar without getting burnt. Explain why it is important to select the correct flame.

6181.statement: Some pupils can't understand that substances can change from one state to another state.
6181.correction: Ensure that the language used is solid state, liquid state and gas state, not solid, liquid and gas.

3577.belief: The idea that there is air between the particles in a gas.
3577.statement: The idea that there is air between the particles in a gas.
3577.correction: Emphasis on explaining that air contains particles and has nothing between them.

7580.statement: Pupils tend to think that all gases are made of air. That gases contain no particles.
7580.correction: Ensure that pupils gain the knowledge that the particles are the substance and between the particles there is nothing.

2779.belief: Evaporation only occurs above the boiling point of a substance.
2779.statement: Evaporation only occurs above the boiling point of a substance.
2779.correction: Give examples of substances other than water.

6965.statement: Pupils mistake common (everyday) usage of pure (i.e. pure orange juice) as being a pure substance when it is, in fact, a mixture.
6965.correction: 'Everyday' usage refers to one source whereas scientific usage refers to particle composition.

7578.statement: Pupils tend to misidentify similar looking apparatus.
7578.correction: Focus on the uses of each apparatus, highlight its distinguishing features to help pupils correctly identify apparatus.

6404.statement: Pupils either put too much or not enough detail into their drawings = muddled representations
6404.correction: Use the 'less is more' approach, and remind pupils to include labels - **clarity is key**. Allows for less detail and avoids any confusion.

6264.statement: Pupils confuse similarly sounding key terms; solute, solvent, solution, soluble, insoluble.
6264.correction: Spend time discussing ways to remember the differences, e.g. solvent has more letters = have more of it in the solution.

5924.belief: Pupil confuse diffusion and Brownian motion.
5924.statement: Pupil confuse diffusion and Brownian motion.
5924.correction: Brownian motion is the random movement of particles due to collisions. Diffusion is due to concentration differences between 2 substances.

3090.belief: Forces of attraction are broken when a substance dissolves.
3090.statement: Forces of attraction are broken when a substance dissolves.
3090.correction: Forces of attraction are *overcome*. They are still acting between the particles, but weaker than before so a different particle arrangement

7576.statement: Pupils tend to confuse independent and dependent variables.
7576.correction: Think of an experiment as "cause and effect." The independent variable is what you change – the cause. The dependent variable is what you measure – the effect of that change.

6882.belief: Sometimes pupils like to write methods in paragraph form, which can be difficult to follow.
6882.statement: Sometimes pupils like to write methods in paragraph form, which can be difficult to follow.
6882.correction: Suggest pupils draw labelled diagrams of key steps, write a sentence to describe each diagram, then go back to number them in order.

7170.statement: Pupils regularly confuse the words 'table' and 'graph'.
7170.correction: Stress that a table of results holds measurements / observations (like a dinner table holds plates), while a graph is only on *graph* paper.

6199.statement: Pupils commonly confuse discrete & continuous data. They also think lines of best fit are straight.
6199.correction: Link *how* the data is collected to the type of data it is. Stress that best fit lines are just that - a best fit - they aren't exact!

7172.statement: Pupils are reluctant/struggle to plot multiple sets of data on one graph.
7172.correction: Fold the table of results so pupils are only looking at one set of data at a time when plotting. Use different plot symbols/colours too.

3197.belief: A funnel is the same as a filter. Dissolved substances will be collected in the filter paper.
3197.statement: A funnel is the same as a filter. Dissolved substances will be collected in the filter paper.
3197.correction: A filter separates materials. Dissolved substances are smaller than the pores in the filter paper and so will pass through with the liquid.

8593.statement: Pupils sometimes use the terms evaporation and boiling interchangeably, but they are not the same.
8593.correction: Boiling: a liquid substance is heated & gas bubbles form. Evaporation: same, BUT only on the surface of the liquid & the gas mixes with air.

2979.belief: Filtration alone can separate salt from rock salt - idea that only one technique is needed.
2979.statement: Filtration alone can separate salt from rock salt - idea that only one technique is needed.
2979.correction: Highlight that each separation technique (so far) creates two products; one of them may still be a mixture that requires further separation.

10017.belief: If a substance cannot be seen, it has disappeared and is no longer present.
10017.statement: If a substance cannot be seen, it has disappeared and is no longer present.
10017.correction: Remind pupils of work regarding evaporation and use particle models to describe / explain what a solution of two liquids is like.

7518.statement: Pupils struggle to understand gas state; thinking solids, liquids and gases as 'types' of matter.
7518.correction: Refer to/use particle models to help clarify different states of matter and use these to describe why separation techniques work.

7887.belief: Heating a substance strongly and for extended periods will improve distillation.
7887.statement: Pupils think that heating a substance strongly and for extended periods will improve distillation.
7887.correction: Stress that distillation is a skill which requires careful control of heating so only one substance is in the condenser at a time.

7412.statement: Pupils can struggle to interpret information that contain several samples on one chromatogram.
7412.correction: Stress a systematic approach to interpreting chromatograms - use rulers. Live model this - using a visualiser helps enormously.

7388.statement: Pupils often struggle with the idea of how small an atom actually is.
7388.correction: Use examples to show how many atoms make up certain things, e.g. a cell or a grain of sand.

9708.statement: Students often confuse the difference between chemical and physical properties.
9708.correction: A chemical property describes how an element will react with other substances. Physical properties describes the appearance and behaviour.

2845.belief: There are exceptions for both metals and non-metals, which have different properties.
2845.statement: There are exceptions for both metals and non-metals, which have different properties.
2845.correction: Use examples such as mercury and graphite in your teaching.

472.belief: Assuming that substances like sodium chloride (NaCl) are diatomic.
472.statement: Assuming that substances like sodium chloride (NaCl) are diatomic.
472.correction: It is very important to emphasise that only non-metals exist as monatomic or molecules.

2625.belief: Elements cannot have metal and non-metal properties.
2625.statement: Elements cannot have metal and non-metal properties.
2625.correction: Introduction of the metalloids and discussion of their properties.

1887.belief: Compounds will have the same properties as the elements from which they are made.
1887.statement: Compounds will have the same properties as the elements from which they are made.
1887.correction: Compounds usually have completely different properties from the elements from which they are made.

11162.belief: Writing subscript values as superscript values.
11162.statement: Writing subscript values as superscript values.
11162.correction: Subscript values show the number of the atoms, while superscript in maths is used to square a value and so does not apply to chemical formulae.

9748.statement: Students often forget to change the non-metal name to either -ide or -ate.
9748.correction: Emphasise when the non-metal reacts with a metal it changes its name to -ide. It is -ate if the non-metal is also bonded to oxygen.

3578.belief: The idea that atoms can be created or destroyed when new products are formed.
3578.statement: The idea that atoms can be created or destroyed when new products are formed.
3578.correction: Matter cannot be created or destroyed, only arranged differently to be formed into new products.

8488.statement: Pupils do not understand chemical reactions as changes, they considered them to be ‘events’. They focus on observable features e.g. colour change rather than formation of a new substance.
8488.correction: Use questioning to encourage pupils to make links between their observations as evidence that a new substance is formed when substances undergo chemical reactions.

6741.statement: Pupils get confused with what numbers can be changed, many of them try to change the subscript numbers in formulae to balance equations.
6741.correction: Use the layout modelled in the slides to go through the examples using the 'circled method' and tell pupils that when adding more of a substance they must add all elements in the substance, e.g. 2MgO = (MgO)(MgO).

7999.statement: Pupils often think that all metals rust.
7999.correction: Explain that rust is a form of iron oxide and show pupils other examples of metal oxides, e.g. copper oxide, to show how different they are.

7523.statement: Pupils struggle to understand that products of water and carbon dioxide are made when combustion takes place as they cannot see them.
7523.correction: Remind pupils about the rule of rearranging atoms from reactants to form products. Use a molecular modelling kit to show the combustion of methane. Remember to balance the reaction so that conservation of mass occurs.

7525.statement: Pupils often struggle to understand that not all reactions consist of two substances mixed together to cause a reaction.
7525.correction: Show the symbol equation and how the reactants are rearranged to form the products.

7528.statement: Pupils can struggle to understand that a solid is not always a large piece of a substance.
7528.correction: Show visually the difference between a transparent coloured solution e.g. copper sulfate solution and a coloured precipitate solution. Practice describing the difference between a white precipitate and a transparent colourless solution.

7575.statement: Pupils tend to classify rocks by colour, shape or size - not useful for distinguishing rock types.
7575.correction: Encourage pupils to focus on the texture of a rock (the grains and how they are arranged) to classify them and consider uses of those rocks.

6732.statement: Pupils generally confuse the distinctions between a rock and a mineral.
6732.correction: Stress and reinforce the definitions of each. Use examples of each and practice classifying them as a mineral or rock.

6670.statement: Pupils sometimes focus on one feature to classify rocks as one type or another.
6670.correction: Stress that the rock classification system is gradual - show examples of various metamorphic rocks, highlighting similarities / differences.

7309.statement: Pupils struggle to appreciate the relative scales between each layer and features of the mantle.
7309.correction: Use common models (boiled egg or an orange) to stress the relative sizes and use multiple demonstrations to model features of the mantle.

7570.statement: Some pupils (and teachers and even textbooks) suggest that plate movement is due solely to convection currents.
7570.correction: Stress that the understanding of what drives of tectonic plate moment is still developing; using demonstrations to reinforce the current understanding of slab pull and ridge push are helpful. Avoid any demos that reinforce ideas the mantle is liquid.

10253.statement: Some think all lavas/magmas are the same and the type of igneous rock formed depends on cooling rate.
10253.correction: Stress that the type of igneous rock formed depends upon the mineral composition of the lava/magma *and* the rate of cooling. Use examples to reinforce this.

5794.belief: Pressure and heating caused by burying alone is enough to cause metamorphism or rock to melt.
5794.statement: Pressure and heating caused by burying alone is enough to cause metamorphism or rock to melt.
5794.correction: Highlight that the temperatures / pressures needed for metamorphism or rocks to melt are typically found at plate boundaries / hot spots.

2660.correction: Remind students about the conservation of energy.

10018.belief: All substances freeze when really cold, like water.
10018.statement: All substances freeze when really cold, like water.
10018.correction: Show state changes using particle diagrams / kinetic energy model. Challenge pupils to identify state given real world temperature data.

2350.belief: The difference between the surroundings (where the reaction takes place, e.g. solution) and the environment (where the reaction mixture is, e.g. classroom). The existence of cold.
2350.statement: The difference between the surroundings (where the reaction takes place, e.g. solution) and the environment (where the reaction mixture is, e.g. classroom). The existence of cold.
2350.correction: Use the separate terms of surroundings and environment throughout the lesson. Explain that thermal energy transfer only takes place from somewhere that is warmer and somewhere that is cooler.

6749.statement: Pupils get easily confused between variables and how to ensure a fair test.
6749.correction: Ensure that pupils understand the independent variable is the type of fuel, the dependent variable is the temperature increase and control variables are mass of fuel and volume of water.

5751.belief: Power stations generate most of the electricity that we use in the UK.
5751.statement: Power stations generate most of the electricity that we use in the UK.
5751.correction: Highlight how over half of UK electricity is now generated using renewable energy resources and that power stations contribute about a third of the electricity. Also highlight the continuing need for power stations due to varying weather and demand.

668.belief: Biomass is a renewable energy resource because plants can be regrown.
668.statement: Biomass is a renewable energy resource because plants can be regrown.
668.correction: Discuss the idea that renewable resources **will not** run out, whereas biomass **could** run out or be seriously depleted if it is not used sustainably.

6739.statement: Pupils can get confused by the litmus paper test and presume that a change has to take place for it to be a positive result.
6739.correction: Use the phrases, stay red, stay blue, turn red, turn blue to help them understand that sometimes a positive test is no colour change.

2341.belief: The difference between concentrated and dilute vs strong and weak when referring to acids and alkalis (not covered in this lesson).
2341.statement: The difference between concentrated and dilute vs strong and weak when referring to acids and alkalis (not covered in this lesson).
2341.correction: For acids and alkalis concentration is the amount of hydrogen dissolved in a certain volume of solution. The higher the concentration, the lower the pH. Strong and weak refer to the ability of an acid to release hydrogen (not covered in lesson).

8200.belief: The red cabbage will change to the same colours as universal indicator solution.
8200.statement: Pupils often think that the red cabbage will change to the same colours as universal indicator solution.
8200.correction: Remind pupils that there are many different indicators used to show different pH.

6420.belief: All reactions will be vigorous and they will see lots of bubbles being formed instantly.
6420.statement: Pupils can expect that all reactions will be vigorous and they will see lots of bubbles being formed instantly.
6420.correction: Get pupils to leave and observe their metal + acid reactions over a period of time, e.g. 5 minutes. This will ensure that they will be able to observe bubbles forming more slowly for metals such as iron or zinc.

6542.statement: Pupils find it difficult to carry out a complex 3-stage practical.
6542.correction: Demonstrate the practical or do a 'follow with me' step-by-step method. If you are short on time you could just carry out the first part of the practical to produce the copper sulfate solution then stop.

8509.statement: Pupils often do not understand what neutralisation is i.e. exactly the correct quantities of components from the acid and base combined to form water.
8509.correction: It is worth emphasising that water is formed and it is this which is neutral as it contains the hydrogen and oxygen atoms from the acid and base.

7597.belief: Acids ‘eat away’ materials and disappear. They observe reactions and see the loss of a reactant, but do not recognise the formation of a new soluble product.
7597.statement: Pupils think that acids ‘eat away’ materials and disappear. They observe reactions and see the loss of a reactant, but do not recognise the formation of a new soluble product.
7597.correction: Ensure that pupils understand the concept of solubility and use the words soluble and dissolve when describing the production of metal salts during these reactions.

11070.belief: The word material can be challenging, it has a different meaning in everyday life. Understanding that an alloy is a mixture and not a compound is hard because the elements are difficult to separate.
11070.statement: The word material can be challenging, it has a different meaning in everyday life. Understanding that an alloy is a mixture and not a compound is hard because the elements are difficult to separate.
11070.correction: Provide lots of different examples of materials and use the word correctly within the scientific contexts. An alloy is the exception to the rule and is separated by thermal or chemical processes.

9878.belief: Intermolecular forces exist within a molecule, unaware of the significant difference in strength between chemical bonds within atoms and the forces between molecules.
9878.statement: Students often think that intermolecular forces exist within a molecule, unaware of the significant difference in strength between chemical bonds within atoms and the forces between molecules.
9878.correction: Help students to make the link between the structure of the polymer and its property by using models. Point out where the intermolecular forces occur and compare this to where the chemical bonds are.

8765.belief: The reactant disappears during the reaction. Acids and metals react because the acid eats away the metal.
8765.statement: The reactant disappears during the reaction. Acids and metals react because the acid eats away the metal.
8765.correction: Use word and symbol equations to reinforce the idea that during the reaction new chemicals are produced from the reactants. Demonstrate that metals less reactive than hydrogen will not react with acid.

10534.belief: Understanding displacement reactions can be challenging as many pupils think the product has moved from somewhere else rather than being produced during the chemical reaction.
10534.statement: Understanding displacement reactions can be challenging as many pupils think the product has moved from somewhere else rather than being produced during the chemical reaction.
10534.correction: Focus on explaining the macroscopic observations in a displacement reaction in terms of chemical change. Then move on to apply the ideas to the reactivity of the metal.

882.belief: The catalyst is one of the reactants and gets used up during the reaction.
882.statement: The catalyst is one of the reactants and gets used up during the reaction.
882.correction: Emphasise that the chemical reaction will take place without the catalyst but at a very slow rate.

6409.statement: Pupils equate 'weathering' as the breakdown of rock caused only by the 'weather'. They also tend to use 'weathering' and 'erosion' interchangeably.
6409.correction: Provide many opportunities for pupils to identify weathering from erosion or classify examples of weathering or erosion.

7719.belief: Compaction and cementation are the same processes.
7719.statement: Some pupils think that compaction and cementation are the same processes.
7719.correction: Highlight that compaction is due to pressure while cementation occurs when minerals act as a 'glue' holding sediments together.

6837.statement: Pupils often interpret the rock cycle as the cause of rock formation.
6837.correction: Stress the rock cycle is a representation of relationships between the rock types. For rocks to change from one type to another requires specific conditions (i.e. igneous rock can change into metamorphic or melted into a different igenous rock).

10286.belief: We can keep finding more fossil fuels to use, and that they are a renewable energy resource.
10286.statement: Thinking we can keep finding more fossil fuels to use, and that they are a renewable energy resource.
10286.correction: Teach that fossil fuels take millions of years to form and they are being used at a faster rate than they are produced.

485.correction: Describe the atmosphere as ~78% unreactive nitrogen and ~20% oxygen. Explain that if the atmosphere were mostly oxygen, the planet would quickly be engulfed in fire.

781.belief: Burning hydrocarbons results in harmless products.
781.statement: Burning hydrocarbons results in harmless products.
781.correction: Teach about carbon dioxide being a greenhouse gas, and the impact on global temperatures.

861.belief: Carbon atoms can be created or destroyed.
861.statement: Carbon atoms can be created or destroyed.
861.correction: Focus teaching on the carbon cycle as a closed system in which the total amount of carbon is constant. Discuss the processes of how carbon is transferred from one place to another, rather than processes of how carbon is lost or gained.

2627.belief: Elements in the same period have similar properties.
2627.statement: Elements in the same period have similar properties.
2627.correction: Properties vary across a period; it is elements in the same group that share similar properties.

3407.belief: Group 2 metals are more reactive than Group 1 because reactivity increases across the groups.
3407.statement: Group 2 metals are more reactive than Group 1 because reactivity increases across the groups.
3407.correction: Group 1 metals are more reactive with water; reactivity increases down a group (for Groups 1 and 2), not along a period.

3438.belief: All halogens are gases at room temperature because they're non-metals; all halogens form toxic compounds.
3438.statement: All halogens are gases at room temperature because they're non-metals; all halogens form toxic compounds.
3438.correction: Not all halogens are gases at room temperature; bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid. Halogens can be toxic in their elemental form or in high concentrations, but they also form essential compounds, like table salt and disinfectants.

1936.belief: Confusing the spelling of "noble" with "Nobel" and misunderstanding why noble gases are named so.
1936.statement: Confusing the spelling of "noble" with "Nobel" and misunderstanding why noble gases are named so.
1936.correction: Clarify that "noble" refers to their stability and lack of reactivity due to a full outer electron shell, meaning they don't need to bond with other elements.

9809.statement: Students often struggle with the idea of how small an atom actually is. In contrast, how small the nucleus is, relative to the size of the atom.
9809.correction: The use of units and numbers to show the difference in size, e.g. the atom is approximately 10, 000 times larger than the nucleus. The radius of the atom is 0.1nm and the nucleus very small compared to that of the atom.

1951.belief: Confusion between the models and the order in which they were conceived. Also, pupils often mix up which subatomic particles are present in each model.
1951.statement: Confusion between the models and the order in which they were conceived. Also, pupils often mix up which subatomic particles are present in each model.
1951.correction: Practise is required listing the key features of each model and the subatomic particles present. A timeline with the key features present helps pupils to understand the process of discovery and how long this can take.

9860.belief: An elemental diatomic molecule, e.g. hydrogen, is a compound because they see two atoms chemically joined together.
9860.statement: Students often think that an elemental diatomic molecule, e.g. hydrogen, is a compound because they see two atoms chemically joined together.
9860.correction: The teacher needs to emphasise the definition for compounds. Molecules are not the same as compounds, some molecules are compounds, not all.

6216.statement: Pupils often confuse the atomic number and mass number with regard to the number of electrons in an atom. They also can confuse the number of electrons which can be held by each shell.
6216.correction: Emphasise that the lower number (atomic number/proton number) represents the number of electrons (reference to the mass being larger can help). Practise as many electron arrangements as possible.

6981.statement: Pupils often mix up the atomic number and atomic mass number and get confused over which subatomic particles these represent.
6981.correction: It helps to describe the atomic number as the proton number to help the pupils remember. Also, the provided periodic tables often have a key to help and this should be highlight to pupils.

9713.statement: Students often confuse the subatomic particle responsible for making an atom an isotope, and how isotopes are responsible for the relative atomic masses to 1 d.p.
9713.correction: Practice determining the number of neutrons in multiple isotopes.

8546.statement: Pupils may use the atomic number rather than mass when calculating the relative formula mass. Also, the number of atoms can be missed for the percentage of an element in a compound.
8546.correction: Emphasise that atomic mass is the larger number for each element on the periodic table and encourage pupils to use the key present to help them identify the mass.

6114.belief: The when the periodic table was devised, scientists knew about the subatomic particles.
6114.statement: Pupils often believe that the when the periodic table was devised, scientists knew about the subatomic particles.
6114.correction: Emphasise when the subatomic particles were discovered in comparison to when Mendeleev devised his periodic table.

489.belief: Atoms react because they 'want' to gain a fuller outer shell of electrons – atoms don't have feelings! Monatomic means one atom and may be confused with the term element, which means one type of atom.
489.statement: Atoms react because they 'want' to gain a fuller outer shell of electrons – atoms don't have feelings! Monatomic means one atom and may be confused with the term element, which means one type of atom.
489.correction: Take care with language and avoid personifying the atoms. Make sure that definitions and terms are used correctly.

4575.belief: A metal is an individual atom. The property of a metal atom is the same as the bulk material. Pupils get confused between the attractive forces in the metal atoms and the metallic bond.
4575.statement: A metal is an individual atom. The property of a metal atom is the same as the bulk material. Pupils get confused between the attractive forces in the metal atoms and the metallic bond.
4575.correction: Reinforce the idea that atoms are tiny and not visible to the naked eye. The material we know as metal is many millions of atoms joined together. Revisit the structure of the atoms before introducing the idea of metallic bonding and giant structure.

4576.belief: The metallic structure model is a replication of reality. Therefore, metals contain seawater. The concept of electric current is challenging. Some may think that electrons jump from atom to atom.
4576.statement: The metallic structure model is a replication of reality. Therefore, metals contain seawater. The concept of electric current is challenging. Some may think that electrons jump from atom to atom.
4576.correction: Discuss why scientists use models with the pupils, explaining that a model is only as good as what it can explain, so it develops over time. Remind pupils how an electric circuit works before discussing why metals are good conductors.

3862.belief: Ions are not formed because atoms 'want' or 'need' a full outer electron shell. Pupils often find standard notation difficult and get confused about when to use superscript and subscript.
3862.statement: Ions are not formed because atoms 'want' or 'need' a full outer electron shell. Pupils often find standard notation difficult and get confused about when to use superscript and subscript.
3862.correction: It is important that pupils understand that atoms do not have 'wants' or 'needs'. Emphasise that the driving force for the formation of atoms is an increase in stability when the outer electron shell is full.

3858.belief: The ionic bond is the transfer of electrons and not the electrostatic forces of attraction between the ions. Dot and cross diagrams show the empirical formula of the lattice and not an ionic molecule.
3858.statement: The ionic bond is the transfer of electrons and not the electrostatic forces of attraction between the ions. Dot and cross diagrams show the empirical formula of the lattice and not an ionic molecule.
3858.correction: Ensure students have a good understanding of how ions are formed, the arrangement of ions in a giant lattice structure and empricial formula before moving on to disucss using dot and cross diagrams to model ionic bonding.

10705.belief: Using ionic charges to determine the empirical formulae, especially with polyatomic ions. Standard notation is difficult and confusing, e.g. when to use superscripts, subscripts or brackets.
10705.statement: Using ionic charges to determine the empirical formulae, especially with polyatomic ions. Standard notation is difficult and confusing, e.g. when to use superscripts, subscripts or brackets.
10705.correction: At this stage, pupils will need to just learn the the formulae of the polyatomic ions and accept that a full explanation will come later in their chemistry learning. Provide pupils with plenty of practice of writing and using ionic formulae.

9226.belief: There are several misconceptions associated with properties such as when something dissolves it disappears, electrical conductivity is a flow of electrons rather than charge.
9226.statement: There are several misconceptions associated with properties such as when something dissolves it disappears, electrical conductivity is a flow of electrons rather than charge.
9226.correction: When discussing electrical conductivity, emphasise the idea of electrical conductivity being a flow charge with ions behaving as charge carriers. The electron transfer that occurs during ion formation is nothing to do with conductivity.

2084.belief: The covalent bond is the shared pair of electrons; both electrons must come from different atoms. The central atom is responsible for the formation of covalent bonds as they want a full outer shell.
2084.statement: The covalent bond is the shared pair of electrons; both electrons must come from different atoms. The central atom is responsible for the formation of covalent bonds as they want a full outer shell.
2084.correction: All chemical bonds are an electrostatic force of attraction between positive and negative charges. The sharing of electrons is the process by which covalent bonds are formed. Avoid using anthropomorphic analogies to explain how covalent bonds form.

7744.belief: Covalent bonds are broken when any covalent structure undergoes a change of state; not just those in giant covalent structures.
7744.statement: Pupils often think that covalent bonds are broken when any covalent structure undergoes a change of state; not just those in giant covalent structures.
7744.correction: Use physical models to show the difference between a simple covalent structure and a giant covalent structure. Explain that it is the weak intermolecular forces that are overcome when a simple covalent molecule changes state.

10540.belief: Understanding that the models used to represent chemical story do not tell the complete story. Different models can be used to explain different aspects of bonding, but they all have limitations.
10540.statement: Understanding that the models used to represent chemical story do not tell the complete story. Different models can be used to explain different aspects of bonding, but they all have limitations.
10540.correction: Avoid telling your class that the model is wrong; rather stress its limitations. Stress the idea that as we learn more about bonding, we will be able to use more sophisticated models to show and explain more key ideas.

8096.belief: The particles are embedded in the substance rather than being the substance. Most pupils think that substances in the liquid state will compress a little.
8096.statement: Pupils often think that the particles are embedded in the substance rather than being the substance. Most pupils think that substances in the liquid state will compress a little.
8096.correction: Reinforce that most substances can exist in all three states of matter and when they are in the gas state there is nothing between the particles but empty space.

8097.belief: The particles within the liquid will have melted or boiled rather than remain the same size and shape, i.e. atoms do not have bulk properties like melting and boiling points.
8097.statement: Pupils often think that the particles within the liquid will have melted or boiled rather than remain the same size and shape, i.e. atoms do not have bulk properties like melting and boiling points.
8097.correction: Ensure that you specifically say that the particles themselves will not melt or boil.

8286.belief: Substances need to be at their boiling point temperature to evaporate.
8286.statement: Pupils think that substances need to be at their boiling point temperature to evaporate.
8286.correction: Use plenty of real life examples of liquids evaporating in situations where pupils know that the liquid is not above its boiling point but still evaporates.

6255.statement: Pupils often confuse physical and chemical changes and think that all particles look and act like those shown in the particle model.
6255.correction: Give the pupils an array of different examples of physical and chemical reactions and get the pupils to consider if new substances have been produced. Show the pupils, using molymods, how different molecules can be.

7344.statement: Pupils can struggle to decide on the scales needed for an axis on a graph.
7344.correction: Suggest a suitable scale that will fit on the graph paper they will use or use a computer to draw graphs.

7529.statement: Pupils struggle to understand what is taking place at the horizontal parts of the graph.
7529.correction: Be concise with your language and ask pupils to use the same language. 'have enough energy to overcome the forces of attraction between particles', 'to slide past each other', 'to move past each other'.

8312.belief: When the temperature is not increasing, i.e. at a change of state, that the experiment is 'not working'.
8312.statement: Pupils can often think that when the temperature is not increasing, i.e. at a change of state, that the experiment is 'not working'.
8312.correction: Question students whilst circulating the class about what they would expect to see and try to get them to imagine what is happening to the particles. Use the heating curve to explain why the temperature did not increase during state changes.

10241.statement: Some think that because a solute can no longer be seen, or that a solvent becomes coloured when a solute dissolves, that the creation of a solution is a chemical change.
10241.correction: Create a salt solution, then evaporate the water (leaving salt crystals) to demonstrate that the salt and water have not chemically combined and therefore dissolving (to create a solution) is a physical change.

3196.belief: A funnel is the same as a filter.
3196.statement: A funnel is the same as a filter.
3196.correction: A funnel streamlines movement, while a filter separates materials. Use everyday examples to highlight the difference, e.g. an oil funnel vs. an oil filter, or a coffee funnel vs. a coffee filter.

7413.statement: Pupils can struggle to interpret information that contains several samples on one chromatogram.
7413.correction: Stress a systematic approach to interpreting chromatograms - use rulers. Live model this - using a visualiser helps enormously.

8500.statement: Pupils to understand gas state; thinking solids, liquids and gases as 'types' of matter.
8500.correction: Refer to/use particle models to help clarify different states of matter and use these to describe why separation techniques work.

3473.belief: Heating a mixture strongly will cause distillation to occur more quickly.
3473.statement: Heating a mixture strongly will cause distillation to occur more quickly.
3473.correction: Heating a mixture strongly could cause multiple components to enter a condenser (or delivery tube), resulting in a contaminated distillate. Careful, gentle heating of the mixture to ensure no bubbles near the condenser will reduce contamination.

7581.statement: Pupils tend to think that all water is the same. Pupils tend to forget that non-visible substances are also found in water.
7581.correction: Stress that pure water only contains H₂O molecules. Other types of water may include varying amounts of dissolved salts, other solids or micro-organisms. Stress that microbes must be killed for water to be potable, but are too difficult to remove.

8366.belief: 'wastewater' is the same as 'sewage' and/or that anything found in a sewer is 'sewage'.
8366.statement: Some pupils think that 'wastewater' is the same as 'sewage' and/or that anything found in a sewer is 'sewage'.
8366.correction: Stress that wastewater is any used water that has been affected by domestic, industrial and agricultural processes; sewage is a part of waste water, but specifically that which is contaminated by with faeces and urine.

10936.belief: All water samples are neutral (i.e. pH of 7).
10936.statement: All water samples are neutral (i.e. pH of 7).
10936.correction: The acidity / alkalinity of water samples is affected by the dissolved substances in each sample.

10934.correction: The dissolved solid content of water samples is affected by the environment from which it was obtained.

10935.correction: If a water sample is impure, the boiling point of water increases. The greater the amount of impurities in a water sample, the larger the temperature range over which it boils.

6400.statement: Pupils *very* easily confuse different types of reactions.
6400.correction: Spend time developing ways to help pupils remember the differences and regularly challenge them to explain why one reaction is the type it is.

7424.statement: Pupils can struggle to link chemical formulae to what is happening on the atomic level and to what they observe during a chemical reaction.
7424.correction: Reinforce via demonstrations, modelling and diagrams via Johnstone's triangle. One simple demo (e.g. magnesium + oxygen) = one model, one diagram and one chemical reaction equation. Use progressively more complicated demos and build up from there.

7695.belief: Chemical formulae can be changed to balance atoms.
7695.statement: Pupils sometimes think that chemical formulae can be changed to balance atoms.
7695.correction: Put boxes around each formula in the equation / pretend there is a bucket of pre-made molecules which they can use to balance the number of atoms on each side. Stress that it takes perseverance and practice before equations are balanced.

7100.statement: Pupils rarely consider the choice of equipment and its link to the accuracy of the data they collect in a practical.
7100.correction: Highlight that equipment with smaller resolution provides more precise measurements, which can decrease the uncertainty of a calculated mean.

7452.statement: Pupils struggle to recall the order of steps required to mathematically process the available information in order to answer the question.
7452.correction: Colour-coding the steps can help pupils remember how many steps are involved. Much practice and perseverance is needed to create and maintain the memory pathway of the mathematical processing.

7171.statement: Pupils regularly think that neutralisation produces a neutral (i.e. pH 7) solution.
7171.correction: Stress that neutralisation occurs from a complete reaction between an acid and base, which usually occurs between strong acids and strong bases. If a weak acid or weak base is used, the salt solution produced may be alkaline or acidic respectively.

5963.statement: Pupils do not always appreciate that safety in the laboratory is a shared responsibility.
5963.correction: Ensure pupils understand the hazards related to both common chemicals and regularly used equipment.

6034.belief: Acids 'eat' away at substances, e.g. acid rain and limestone, rather than understanding that this is a chemical reaction.
6034.statement: Pupils often believe that acids 'eat' away at substances, e.g. acid rain and limestone, rather than understanding that this is a chemical reaction.
6034.correction: Using familiar reactions between acids and bases, e.g. hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide or calcium carbonate, will provide evidence that a reaction has taken place (i.e. a change in temperature or producing a gas).

6695.statement: Pupils often forget that gases are produced when metals and metal carbonates react with acids.
6695.correction: Emphasise the tests for the gases as a way to remember that they are produced. Writing balanced symbol equations also helps as the pupils can see what elements would be present in the products formed.

6219.statement: Pupils often confuse the chemical definitions for 'concentration' and 'strength'.
6219.correction: Stress that concentration is a measure of particles interspersed throughout a specific volume of liquid.

3741.belief: All indicators provide precise pH values and give the same information as pH meters.
3741.statement: All indicators provide precise pH values and give the same information as pH meters.
3741.correction: Indicators do not provide exact pH values; they only indicate whether a solution is acidic, neutral, or alkaline by changing colour. A pH meter, on the other hand, measures the exact pH value of a solution and is more accurate.

9064.belief: All salts are either completely soluble or completely insoluble in water.
9064.statement: All salts are either completely soluble or completely insoluble in water.
