9064.correction: Not all salts follow a strict 'soluble' or 'insoluble' rule. Some salts have limited solubility, meaning they dissolve only to a certain extent. Solubility rules help us predict the solubility of common salts, but there are always exceptions.

8511.statement: Pupils often do not understand that observing excess metal oxide in the reaction mixture means that the acid has fully reacted.
8511.correction: Emphasise how to observe the end of the reaction and what these observations mean, i.e. excess metal oxide in the reaction mixture or using pH paper to indicate the solution is neutral. Both are evidence of the acid having fully reacted.

6968.statement: Pupils can sometimes mistake the excess base for the salt formed as it is a solid.
6968.correction: Emphasise at the beginning of the experiment what soluble means and that the salt will be initially obtained dissolved in water.

107.belief: All added calcium hydroxide dissolves completely, and the pH readings are accurate without consistent mixing.
107.statement: All added calcium hydroxide dissolves completely, and the pH readings are accurate without consistent mixing.
107.correction: Calcium hydroxide has low solubility in water, so not all of it dissolves readily. Consistent mixing ensures uniform pH readings. Without proper mixing, pH readings can be inaccurate, leading to incorrect conclusions about the neutralisation point.

7058.statement: Pupils often overshoot the end point, especially on their first attempt at a titration.
7058.correction: Pupils will need to work on their dexterity, often with a partner, to ensure the flow of titrant is slow enough from the burette, and that their swirling technique allows ample mixing of the solutions.

6134.belief: Any small colour change signals the end point, leading to inaccurate titrations.
6134.statement: Pupils often believe that any small colour change signals the end point, leading to inaccurate titrations.
6134.correction: Emphasise the importance of adding the titrant drop by drop near the end point and ensure pupils understand that the end point is reached only when the colour change is persistent.

488.belief: Atoms are often anthropomorphised, described as 'wanting' full shells. This implies intent and oversimplifies chemical bonding.
488.statement: Atoms are often anthropomorphised, described as 'wanting' full shells. This implies intent and oversimplifies chemical bonding.
488.correction: Focus on the tendency of atoms to fill their outer shell to 8 electrons to become stable. Emphasise carbon atoms do this by sharing electrons in covalent bonds.

9840.belief: All carbon forms are alike, ignoring structure's impact on properties.
9840.statement: Students may think all carbon forms are alike, ignoring structure's impact on properties.
9840.correction: Emphasise structure-property relationships. Use models to show how diamond's and graphite's differing bonds affect their characteristics.

2085.belief: Covalent bonds break in simple molecules for substances to melt/boil, because this happens in giant covalent structures.
2085.statement: Covalent bonds break in simple molecules for substances to melt/boil, because this happens in giant covalent structures.
2085.correction: Highlight that bonds require large amounts of energy to break, hence the very high melting points of diamond and graphite. As all atoms are bonded these must be broken to melt/boil.

9839.belief: All carbon allotropes have giant covalent structures due to strong covalent bonds.
9839.statement: Students may think all carbon allotropes have giant covalent structures due to strong covalent bonds.
9839.correction: Emphasise that fullerenes and nanotubes, unlike graphene and diamond, have discrete molecular structures.

9838.belief: All carbon allotrope discoveries were recent and that these materials are primarily used in cutting-edge, futuristic applications.
9838.statement: Students may think that all carbon allotrope discoveries were recent and that these materials are primarily used in cutting-edge, futuristic applications.
9838.correction: Emphasise the timeline of discoveries (graphite > fullerenes > nanotubes > graphene), highlighting theoretical predictions preceding isolation. Discuss current uses (e.g. nanotubes in sporting equipment) alongside potential future breakthroughs.

9921.belief: The prefix hydro- in the term hydrocarbons means they contain water; also that hydrocarbons and crude oil are synonymous.
9921.statement: Students often think that the prefix hydro- in the term hydrocarbons means they contain water; also that hydrocarbons and crude oil are synonymous.
9921.correction: Use diagrams to show hydrocarbon composition and compare crude oil to pure hydrocarbons, highlighting the difference visually.

3861.belief: Ionic substances are binary compounds. Bonding and structure are the same thing. Only bonding influences properties.
3861.statement: Ionic substances are binary compounds. Bonding and structure are the same thing. Only bonding influences properties.
3861.correction: As well as multiple ions in ionic substances, there can be polyatomic ions too. Bonding informs structure, and bonding and structure together influences properties.

8029.belief: All nanoparticles are hazardous without considering their varied applications and benefits.
8029.statement: Pupils might think all nanoparticles are hazardous without considering their varied applications and benefits.
8029.correction: Clarify that while nanoparticles may pose risks, they also offer significant benefits in medicine, technology, and environmental protection, with risks varying by type and usage.

7408.statement: Pupils struggle to identify the surroundings in exothermic and endothermic reactions and why the temperature decreases in endothermic reactions when energy is transferred into the reaction.
7408.correction: Explain that the surroundings are where you are making the temperature measurements and that the energy is transferred from the thermal energy store of the surroundings to the chemical energy store of the reaction.

6940.statement: Pupils often measure the final temperature of the reaction mixture rather than the highest temperature.
6940.correction: Encourage pupils to keep monitoring the temperature until it starts to decrease; that way they will know they have seen the highest temperature.

5978.belief: Any decrease in temperature occurring when excess reactant is added to an exothermic reaction is because the reaction has become endothermic.
5978.statement: Pupils can assume that any decrease in temperature occurring when excess reactant is added to an exothermic reaction is because the reaction has become endothermic.
5978.correction: Explain that once the limiting reactant has been used up the exothermic reaction is complete. The addition of excess reactant will only act to cool down the reaction mixture.

6229.statement: Pupils often confuse energy with temperature and therefore expect the products to be higher than the reactants for exothermic reactions i.e. due to temperature increase, and lower for endothermic.
6229.correction: It is useful to discuss the energy transfers occurring during the reaction e.g. exothermic reactions involve the reactant's chemical energy store converting to a smaller chemical energy store in the products and a thermal energy store.

6237.statement: Pupils often confuse the ideas that bonds require energy to break i.e. endothermic process and that energy is released forming bonds i.e. exothermic process.
6237.correction: Bonds will not break unless energy is absorbed to do so. The formation of a bond releases energy to the surroundings.

795.belief: To calculate the instantaneous rate of reaction by reading values from the graph at a specific time.
795.statement: To calculate the instantaneous rate of reaction by reading values from the graph at a specific time.
795.correction: Students need to draw a tangent in order to calculate the gradient of the graph at a specific time to work out the instantaneous rate of reaction.

10301.belief: Precise and accurate are the same thing.
10301.statement: Thinking that precise and accurate are the same thing.
10301.correction: It may help to draw a bullseye target board. Precise results will all be close to each other but may not be near the bullseye. Accurate results will be near the bullseye but may be more scattered if they are not precise.

1758.belief: Every collision between reactant particles results in a chemical reaction.
1758.statement: That every collision between reactant particles results in a chemical reaction.
1758.correction: The slide deck addresses that not every collision between reactant particles results in a chemical reaction. The particles must collide with the activation energy in order for the collision to be successful and a new product be formed.

4036.belief: A larger surface area produces a larger volume/mass of product.
4036.statement: That a larger surface area produces a larger volume/mass of product.
4036.correction: The experiment should help pupils realise they produce the same mass of carbon dioxide when using the same mass of calcium carbonate chips and powder.

6243.statement: Pupils often confuse the mean rate of reaction with the instantaneous rate of reaction, thinking they are the same or not understanding the distinction between the two.
6243.correction: The tasks give pupils s the opportunity to distinguish between mean and instantaneous rate of reaction by calculating both from the same set of data.

10275.belief: As the concentration of a solution in excess changes, so does the volume of gas produced.
10275.statement: Thinking that as the concentration of a solution in excess changes, so does the volume of gas produced.
10275.correction: The slide deck uses graphical data to show that the same volume of gas is produced when different concentrations are used, so long as the reacting solution is in excess.

8766.belief: The reaction stops when the 'X' is no longer visible.
8766.statement: The reaction stops when the 'X' is no longer visible.
8766.correction: The disappearance of the cross only indicates that the sulfur precipitate has formed sufficiently to obscure the cross. The reaction itself continues beyond this point until all reactants are consumed.

3729.belief: Increasing the temperature increases the rate product is formed, and therefore think a faster reaction produces more product.
3729.statement: Increasing the temperature increases the rate product is formed, and therefore think a faster reaction produces more product.
3729.correction: Increasing the temperature will make the reaction proceed faster but will not change the amount of product formed. The reactants are the limiting factor, not the temperature.

110.belief: Adding a bung to the top of a conical flask does not affect volume measurements.
110.statement: Adding a bung to the top of a conical flask does not affect volume measurements.
110.correction: The bung can displace a small volume of gas, which can affect the accuracy of the measurements. It is essential to account for the volume displaced by the bung in calculations.

883.belief: Catalysts increase the amount of product formed.
883.statement: Catalysts increase the amount of product formed.
883.correction: Catalysts do not affect the quantity of products formed. They increase the rate at which the products are formed.

6541.statement: Pupils often find it difficult to apply what they have learnt about alloys when asked about an unfamiliar one, or when provided with a table of data.
6541.correction: Provide pupils with a range of different examples of alloys. Give them plenty of practice of comparing the properties of the alloy with those of the pure metal.

6401.statement: Pupils easily confuse empirical and molecular formula.
6401.correction: Provide multiple examples of formula and challenge pupils to distinguish them as molecular or empirical formula; if the former, push pupils to suggest the molecule's empirical formula.

8248.belief: Simply ensuring a fair test will improve data collecting in a practical.
8248.statement: Pupils think that simply ensuring a fair test will improve data collecting in a practical.
8248.correction: Evaluating a practical is an often overlooked skill. Challenge pupils to focus on the equipment chosen and/or the method followed to consider how better data might be collected.

7530.statement: Pupils sometimes struggle to understand how using different mobile and/or stationary phases affects the resulting chromatograms.
7530.correction: Perform chromatography of the same mixture using different mobile phases/stationary phases and discuss the pros/cons of each combination.

5017.belief: The number one mole represents can be difficult for pupils to grasp and appreciate.
5017.statement: The number one mole represents can be difficult for pupils to grasp and appreciate.
5017.correction: Show many real world examples of 6.02 × 10²³ examples of something - that many basketballs would form a planet the size of the Earth.

6973.statement: Pupils mistake that the same mass of different substances = the same number of particles.
6973.correction: This activity reinforces the mathematical relationship between relative formula mass of a substance, the number of particles present and the mass measured in the lab.

7425.statement: Pupils struggle to link a mole to number of particles.
7425.correction: Use real world examples of converting volumes / masses into number of particles so pupils become more comfortable converting between moles, number of particles particles and masses.

6434.statement: Pupils sometimes fail to understand that excess reactant particles remain in the reaction mixture after the reaction.
6434.correction: Provide a balanced equation and challenge pupils to draw diagrams of a final mixture, stressing that excess particles would also be present. Challenge pupils to consider how the product could be extracted from the excess particles.

6813.statement: Some pupils incorrectly interpret subscript and stoichiometric values in a balanced symbol equation.
6813.correction: Both subscript and stoichiometric values represent ratios. Subscripts indicate ratios *within* substances; stoichiometry. Molar ratios *between* substances in a reaction. Much practice distinguishing between/ interpreting these is time well spent.

7519.statement: Pupils sometimes struggle to understand that 'heating to constant mass' takes time and multiple measurements.
7519.correction: Link the idea that atoms rearrange during a reaction and that for all atoms of a substance to be oxidised, enough oxygen must be present. If the product measurements show a 'constant mass' we can be confident that complete oxidation has occurred.

7990.belief: The mass of the crucible and contents will not change during the reaction because the lid is closed, believing that all gases produced remain inside.
7990.statement: Pupils may think that the mass of the crucible and contents will not change during the reaction because the lid is closed, believing that all gases produced remain inside.
7990.correction: Explain that even with the crucible lid on, gases like carbon dioxide & water vapour formed during decomposition can escape around the edges. This leads to a decrease in mass, which is crucial for calculating the stoichiometry based on the mass loss.

7197.statement: Pupils sometimes rush these calculations and forget to take note of the units.
7197.correction: Remind pupils that units provide the comparison standard for values. Much practice ensuring the correct molar gas volume value is used in calculations is necessary.

8563.statement: Pupils use an incorrect mathematical relationship to calculate the number of moles in a sample.
8563.correction: Depending on the type of substance (solid, solution or gas) a specific mathematical relationship for moles must be used. Challenge pupils to classify substances as (s), (aq), or (g) and apply correct mathematical relationship.

3860.belief: Ionic equations only include ions involved in the reaction, not all ions in the reaction mixture.
3860.statement: Ionic equations only include ions involved in the reaction, not all ions in the reaction mixture.
3860.correction: Stress the difference between reacting ions and spectator ions.

6220.statement: Pupils often confuse the chemistry meaning of strong/weak and concentrated/dilute due to the use of these words in everyday conversation.
6220.correction: Clear definitions of the words are required with practice opportunities to recognise/describe whether the substances are strong or weak acids and if concentrated or dilute.

8599.statement: Pupils use all of their titration results to calculate an average volume used during titration. Pupils also tend to miss steps in this multi-step process.
8599.correction: Stress the need to use concordant results when calculating an average volume for neutralising a solution via titration. Use a calculation grid to help keep each calculation step clearly organised.

6924.statement: Pupils often make mistakes when identifying the different types of bonds and the number of each in a molecule. They may also reverse the calculation of the overall energy change, as make - break.
6924.correction: Molecules can be complex and should be drawn to show all the bonds. Emphasis that double and triple covalent bonds are different to single bonds. Pupils should be instructed to consider whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

9704.statement: Students believing that sustainability is someone else's responsibility.
9704.correction: Everyone needs to reduce, reuse and recycle to ensure sustainable development. The slide deck gives examples of products that can be recycled and the benefits of reducing, reusing and recycling.

9868.belief: Fractional distillation produces new substances from crude oil.
9868.statement: Some students may think that fractional distillation produces new substances from crude oil.
9868.correction: It is important to emphasise that crude oil is a mixture, and the process of fractional distillation is to separate out the different hydrocarbons based on their boiling points.

2090.belief: Cracking is the same as fractional distillation.
2090.statement: Cracking is the same as fractional distillation.
2090.correction: Fractional distillation separates hydrocarbons based on their boiling points. Cracking alters the molecular formula of compounds.

3690.belief: Not including the bonds either side of the repeating unit.
3690.statement: Not including the bonds either side of the repeating unit.
3690.correction: The slide deck states the need for open bonds to show how repeating units are bonded to each other.

10288.belief: A metal and acid react together to produce salt and water.
10288.statement: Thinking that a metal and acid react together to produce salt and water.
10288.correction: Use symbol equations to show how hydrogen is produced, rather than water, due to the absence of oxygen atoms.

10292.belief: Oxidation and reduction are only to do with the loss and gain of oxygen.
10292.statement: Thinking that oxidation and reduction are only to do with the loss and gain of oxygen.
10292.correction: Oxidation is the loss of electrons or the gain of oxygen. Reduction is the gain of electrons or loss of oxygen.

4056.belief: LCAs only measure the carbon footprint of a product.
4056.statement: LCAs only measure the carbon footprint of a product.
4056.correction: The slide deck addresses what is included in a LCA such as energy use, water use and pollutants released.

9552.belief: Spelling of noble re- Nobel and the concept of why they were given this name, i.e. due to having a full outer shell of electrons which means they do not need to bond with other elements.
9552.statement: Spelling of noble re- Nobel and the concept of why they were given this name, i.e. due to having a full outer shell of electrons which means they do not need to bond with other elements.
9552.correction: Explain that the name noble was due to the fact that they are so unreactive and did not need to bond with other elements due to already having a full outer shell of electrons making them so stable.

6281.statement: Pupils can confuse the trend in reactivity down the group.
6281.correction: The practical reacting the metals with water helps to memorably demonstrate the trend, however it is important to ensure that pupils can explain why this happens.

6696.statement: Pupils often forget that the halogens are diatomic molecules.
6696.correction: Explanation of the bonding to form molecules helps to explain why they exist as diatomic molecules.

3437.belief: Halogen solutions are coloured and sometimes it can be difficult to determine colour changes during displacement reactions.
3437.statement: Halogen solutions are coloured and sometimes it can be difficult to determine colour changes during displacement reactions.
3437.correction: Displacement of iodine gives the darkest colour change (turns brown), while bromine will provide one which is lighter (turns orange).

486.belief: The atmosphere is mostly oxygen. The same atmospheric conditions exist at all heights.
486.statement: The atmosphere is mostly oxygen. The same atmospheric conditions exist at all heights.
486.correction: Explain that the atmosphere is ~80% nitrogen and ~20% oxygen. Discuss how atmospheric conditions vary with altitude, affecting oxygen availability.

2559.belief: Earth's atmosphere has always contained oxygen. The atmosphere's composition is static and unchanging.
2559.statement: Earth's atmosphere has always contained oxygen. The atmosphere's composition is static and unchanging.
2559.correction: Clarify the development of oxygen through photosynthesis. Describe how atmospheric composition has evolved over time due to geological and biological processes.

1773.belief: All combustion is complete, producing only CO₂ and water.
1773.statement: All combustion is complete, producing only CO₂ and water.
1773.correction: Highlight the differences between complete and incomplete combustion.

3763.belief: Only industrial activities contribute to atmospheric pollution. Atmospheric pollutants are always visible.
3763.statement: Only industrial activities contribute to atmospheric pollution. Atmospheric pollutants are always visible.
3763.correction: Discuss natural sources of pollutants, like volcanoes. Explain that many harmful pollutants are invisible.

74.belief: Acid rain is immediately harmful to human skin. Acid rain's effects are quick and devastating.
74.statement: Acid rain is immediately harmful to human skin. Acid rain's effects are quick and devastating.
74.correction: Educate that acid rain is less acidic than household acids. Discuss the long-term ecological and structural impacts of acid rain.

3399.belief: All greenhouse gases are artificial and harmful. Increasing any greenhouse gas is bad.
3399.statement: All greenhouse gases are artificial and harmful. Increasing any greenhouse gas is bad.
3399.correction: Emphasise and explain the natural occurrence and necessity of greenhouse gases. Discuss the effect of human activity increasing amounts of greenhouse gases at a very fast rate.

5556.belief: Plants can absorb all of the carbon dioxide that human activity adds to the atmosphere.
5556.statement: Plants can absorb all of the carbon dioxide that human activity adds to the atmosphere.
5556.correction: Talk to the pupils about what happens to the carbon dioxide absorbed by plants so that they understand how the size and number of plants determine the maximum amount of carbon dioxide they can store.

1713.belief: Climate change only leads to hotter weather. Human activity has a negligible impact on climate change.
1713.statement: Climate change only leads to hotter weather. Human activity has a negligible impact on climate change.
1713.correction: Explain the diverse effects of climate change, including extreme weather. Highlight the significant role of human activity in accelerating climate change.

3756.belief: As individuals we are helpless in combatting climate change. Technology alone can solve climate issues.
3756.statement: As individuals we are helpless in combatting climate change. Technology alone can solve climate issues.
3756.correction: Emphasise the impact of collective individual actions, especially in supporting national and international actions (including legislation) that cause appropriate change.

5290.belief: Ozone layer and climate change are linked/the same thing.
5290.statement: Ozone layer and climate change are linked/the same thing.
5290.correction: Ozone layer depletion was caused by human activity, but not through use of burning fossil fuels/greenhouse gas emissions. Both are atmospheric issues, but not the same issue.

6240.statement: Pupils often confuse key terminology, as many words are similar, and confuse electrolysis with physical methods of separation.
6240.correction: Emphasise the keywords and provide plenty of opportunity for them to be used in the correct context. Compare electrolysis to physical methods of separation, such as filtration, and explain that chemical reactions occur at the electrodes.

7800.belief: That, during electrolysis, the charge carriers are electrons and not ions.
7800.statement: Pupils often think that, during electrolysis, the charge carriers are electrons and not ions.
7800.correction: Revisit the structure of ionic compounds in the solid and liquid states. Point out that there are no delocalised electrons. The electrons are associated with ions and so are unable to move through the electrolyte. Ions can move in the liquid state.

10542.belief: Understanding why carbon dioxide is produced at the anode, when there is no carbon in aluminium oxide.
10542.statement: Understanding why carbon dioxide is produced at the anode, when there is no carbon in aluminium oxide.
10542.correction: Remind students of previous knowledge about combustion reactions. Help them to apply this knowledge to this new situation in the electrolysis cell.

8798.belief: Recognising the particles present in an aqueous solution is problematic. Understanding how an electric current flows through an electrolyte is confusing as ions, not electrons, are the charge carrier.
8798.statement: Recognising the particles present in an aqueous solution is problematic. Understanding how an electric current flows through an electrolyte is confusing as ions, not electrons, are the charge carrier.
8798.correction: Ensure that pupils have a good understanding of key terms such as atom, ion, electron, solutions and reactivity before moving on to the electrolysis of aqueous solutions.

6615.statement: Pupils find it hard to remember what is formed at each electrode.
6615.correction: Remind pupils about the electrolysis rules and provide opportunities for them to apply the rules to different electrolytes. Use animations to show the ions present in brine and how they move in the electrolysis cell.

5960.statement: Pupils do not always appreciate the difference between using inert carbon electrodes and metal electrodes, which will take part in the reaction.
5960.correction: Provide pupils with the opportunity to investigate the electrolysis of copper sulfate with both inert electrodes and with copper electrodes and then compare the results.

1933.belief: Confusing the electrodes, electrical cables or carbon electrodes having a break in them.
1933.statement: confusing the electrodes, electrical cables or carbon electrodes having a break in them
1933.correction: Use the PANIC acronym; positive anode negative is cathode. Check all components of the electric circuit.

10541.belief: Understanding which way the electrons flow in the electric cell and explaining why the voltage is sometimes recorded as negative.
10541.statement: Understanding which way the electrons flow in the electric cell and explaining why the voltage is sometimes recorded as negative.
10541.correction: The more reactive metal is always oxidised, i.e. looses electrons which flow towards the less reactive metal. Demonstrate that a negative voltage is seen when the electrical leads connected to the voltmeter are swapped around.

1932.belief: Confusing electrode reactions with those that occur in electrolysis. For example in a hydrogen fuel cell, hydrogen is oxidised at the anode but in electrolysis, hydrogen is produced at the cathode.
1932.statement: Confusing electrode reactions with those that occur in electrolysis. For example in a hydrogen fuel cell, hydrogen is oxidised at the anode but in electrolysis, hydrogen is produced at the cathode.
1932.correction: Discuss the electrode reactions in terms of electron loss or gain; rather that just relying on memory. This will provide pupils with the tools to work out the electrode reactions.

9890.belief: All metals react vigorously with water, and may believe all transition metals form only one type of ion, and might think that all metals are equally good catalysts.
9890.statement: Students may think all metals react vigorously with water, and may believe all transition metals form only one type of ion, and might think that all metals are equally good catalysts.
9890.correction: Unlike Group 1 metals, transition metals react slowly with water or not at all. Transition metals can form ions with different charges, leading to compounds with varying properties and colours. Each reaction will be catalysed best by one catalyst.

9699.belief: Rusting refers to the oxidation of any metal, and that corrosion is linked to the hazard 'corrosive'.
9699.statement: Students often believe rusting refers to the oxidation of any metal, and that corrosion is linked to the hazard 'corrosive'.
9699.correction: Highlight the conditions required for rusting, and the general description of corrosion.

8215.belief: A reversible reaction will always go to completion in one direction before reversing.
8215.statement: Pupils often think that a reversible reaction will always go to completion in one direction before reversing.
8215.correction: Explain that in a reversible reaction, if the conditions allow it, both the forward and backward reaction can occur at the same time.

2720.belief: Equilibrium can occur in an open system; no reactions occur at equilibrium; amounts of reactants and products are equal at equilibrium.
2720.statement: Equilibrium can occur in an open system; no reactions occur at equilibrium; amounts of reactants and products are equal at equilibrium.
2720.correction: Equilibrium requires a closed system; in an open system, matter exchange disrupts balance. At equilibrium, reactions still occur but at equal rates, leading to constant amounts, not necessarily equal amounts of reactants and products.

9743.statement: Students find it difficult to understand why continuous removal of ammonia is required to increase yield.
9743.correction: Highlight that the Haber Process is a dynamic equilibrium. If ammonia is not continuously removed, the equilibrium will shift back towards the reactants, reducing the yield.

6253.statement: Pupils often confuse percentage yield with atom economy, thinking both measure the same efficiency aspect.
6253.correction: Clarify that percentage yield measures actual vs. theoretical product amount, while atom economy measures reactants' mass converted to desired product.

3487.belief: Higher temperature/pressure always increases the yield of products in equilibrium reactions.
3487.statement: Higher temperature/pressure always increases the yield of products in equilibrium reactions.
3487.correction: High temperature can decrease yield in exothermic reactions by shifting equilibrium toward reactants; high pressures can decrease yield where there are fewer gaseous moles of reactants than products.

7612.belief: Ammonia is safe to handle without precautions because it's a common household chemical.
7612.statement: Pupils may think ammonia is safe to handle without precautions because it's a common household chemical.
7612.correction: Emphasise ammonia's toxicity and the importance of using PPE and proper ventilation.

240.belief: Ammonia and ammonium are the same thing.
240.statement: Ammonia and ammonium are the same thing.
240.correction: Carefully compare the different chemical formulae, structures, and distinct uses in fertilisers vs. industrial applications. Use visual aids to reinforce these differences.

9873.statement: Students often think: all glass types have the same properties and uses; polyethene types are identical in structure and use; and composites are simple mixtures (not engineered materials).
9873.correction: Clarify that soda-lime and borosilicate glass differ in production and use. Explain the distinct processes and uses of LDPE and HDPE. Describe how composites are engineered to achieve specific properties.

3043.belief: Flame colours are unique, even in mixtures.
3043.statement: Flame colours are unique, even in mixtures.
3043.correction: Explain that strong colours, like sodium's yellow, can mask others. Use spectrometry to identify masked elements.

10993.belief: All white precipitates in chemical tests indicate the presence of the same ion without the need for further testing.
10993.statement: All white precipitates in chemical tests indicate the presence of the same ion without the need for further testing.
10993.correction: Explain that white precipitates can indicate different ions depending on the test. For instance, barium sulfate indicates sulfate ions, silver chloride indicates chloride ions, and sodium hydroxide tests distinguish between cations.

10199.belief: All tests for ions are interchangeable and can be used in any order without affecting the outcome.
10199.statement: All tests for ions are interchangeable and can be used in any order without affecting the outcome.
10199.correction: Clarify that each test is specific and must be conducted in a particular order to avoid interference. For example, testing for sulfates before halides can prevent false positives caused by overlapping precipitates, ensuring accurate identification.

9267.belief: The shortest alkene is one containing only one carbon atom.
9267.statement: The shortest alkene is one containing only one carbon atom.
9267.correction: Teach that alkenes contain the C=C bond and therefore the shortest alkene is ethene.

3723.belief: Incorrectly writing the molecular formula of alcohols.
3723.statement: Incorrectly writing the molecular formula of alcohols.
3723.correction: Help pupils understand the difference between structural formula, e.g C₂H₅OH, and molecular formula, e.g C₂H₆O.

2256.belief: Describing the colour change of bromine water with an alkene from orange to clear.
2256.statement: Describing the colour change of bromine water with an alkene from orange to clear.
2256.correction: Coloured solutions can be clear if you can see through them. Colourless means it has no colour. Bromine water in the presence of an alkene changes from orange to colourless.

1930.belief: Confusing the concentration and strength of acids.
1930.statement: Confusing the concentration and strength of acids.
1930.correction: Clearly define a strong and weak acid.

3691.belief: Not including the bonds at the end of a repeating unit.
3691.statement: Not including the bonds at the end of a repeating unit.
3691.correction: The slide deck states the need for open bonds to show how repeating units are bonded to each other.

10298.belief: The polymer identification codes mean that all these polymers can be recycled as the symbols look similar to the recycling symbol.
10298.statement: Thinking that the polymer identification codes mean that all these polymers can be recycled as the symbols look similar to the recycling symbol.
10298.correction: Only some polymers can be recycled. These normally have the code 1 or 2.

10276.belief: DNA is made of a single polymer chain.
10276.statement: Thinking that DNA is made of a single polymer chain.
10276.correction: Use the slides and a model to reinforce that DNA contains two polymer chains in a double helix structure.

7998.belief: All metals react vigorously with water, and may believe all transition metals form only one type of ion, and might think that all metals are equally good catalysts.
7998.statement: Pupils may think all metals react vigorously with water, and may believe all transition metals form only one type of ion, and might think that all metals are equally good catalysts.
7998.correction: Unlike Group 1 metals, transition metals react slowly with water or not at all. Transition metals can form ions with different charges, leading to compounds with varying properties and colours. Each reaction will be catalysed best by one catalyst.

3099.belief: Forgetting to measure the initial mass of the burner and initial temperature of the water.
3099.statement: Forgetting to measure the initial mass of the burner and initial temperature of the water.
3099.correction: Emphasise the importance in remembering to measure this data when writing a method for this practical.

3859.belief: All ionic compounds dissociate completely in aqueous solutions.
3859.statement: All ionic compounds dissociate completely in aqueous solutions.
3859.correction: Not all ionic compounds dissociate completely in water; some may not dissolve at all. It's important to know the solubility rules to correctly predict the behaviour of compounds in solution.

5377.belief: All peaks in a mass spectrum represent intact (and neutral) molecules or atoms.
5377.statement: All peaks in a mass spectrum represent intact (and neutral) molecules or atoms.
5377.correction: Clarify that in mass spectrometry, all detected peaks represent ionised species, not neutral molecules or atoms. The peaks can correspond to either the molecular ion (M⁺) or smaller ionised fragments, as well as different isotopes of an element.

9272.belief: To show the spectator ions in an ionic equation.
9272.statement: To show the spectator ions in an ionic equation.
9272.correction: Spectator ions are ions that remain the same throughout a reaction. They are not included in the ionic equation.

9806.statement: Students struggle to distinguish between phytomining and bioleaching.
9806.correction: Reinforce that the term 'phyto' is a combining form meaning 'plant'.

6251.statement: Pupils can confuse oxidation and reduction when involving electrons. They often mistake a positive charge on an ion as meaning electrons have been added and vice versa for negative ions.
6251.correction: It is very important to teach from first principles what causes the charges and then work up to half equations where the pupils can see the electrons in the equations, finally combining these to form ionic equations.

3294.belief: Getting the electrons confused; how many and which side of the half equations to write them on.
3294.statement: Getting the electrons confused; how many and which side of the half equations to write them on.
3294.correction: When writing a half equation, electrons should be added and not taken away and so should go on the side of the equation where they are added. All charges must cancel each other out and the atoms on each side of the equation balance.

2529.belief: At dynamic equilibrium the reactions stop; increasing pressure always shifts equilibrium to one side; increasing temperature always favours product formation; catalysts shift the equilibrium position.
2529.statement: At dynamic equilibrium the reactions stop; increasing pressure always shifts equilibrium to one side; increasing temperature always favours product formation; catalysts shift the equilibrium position.
2529.correction: At dynamic equilibrium, reactions continue at equal rates. Pressure shifts equilibrium only if gas molecule numbers differ. Temperature favours the endothermic direction when increased. Catalysts speed up reaching equilibrium but don't shift it.

10299.belief: All polymers are only made up of one monomer. Also, confusing condensation reactions to think that it means to condense and take up less space.
10299.statement: Thinking that all polymers are only made up of one monomer. Also, confusing condensation reactions to think that it means to condense and take up less space.
10299.correction: Examples are shown where more than one monomer is used to make condensation polymers. Discuss what condensation is, and how condensation polymerisation produces water or other small molecules depending on the monomers used.

9805.statement: Students struggle to distinguish between phytoextraction and bioleaching.
9805.correction: Reinforce that the term 'phyto' is a combining form meaning 'plant'.

9673.belief: The production of sulfuric acid in the Contact Process is a one-step process (similar to the Haber process).
9673.statement: Students often assume that the production of sulfuric acid in the Contact Process is a one-step process (similar to the Haber process).
9673.correction: Clarify that the Contact Process involves multiple stages, each requiring specific conditions. Emphasise the importance of these conditions in maximising yield and minimising energy consumption.

9711.statement: Students often confuse percentage yield with atom economy, thinking both measure the same efficiency aspect.
9711.correction: Clarify that percentage yield measures actual vs. theoretical product amount, while atom economy measures reactants' mass converted to desired product.
